headline: The Ultrasonic Cleaner That Clears Denture Pores
alt_hooks: I was standing by lane eight with a bottle of lane wax when my upper plate sent a jolt of fire straight through the roof of my mouth.

My granddaughter offered me a bite of her orange popsicle on the back porch, and the look of sheer terror on my face made her start crying.
script:
Three tubes of pink adhesive every single month.

Thirty-six tubes a year stacked in my bathroom cabinet like caulk.

For two years, the roof of my mouth felt like someone held a hot iron to it.

I could not eat a fresh tomato from my garden.

A single orange wedge made my eyes water from the stinging burn.

Let me back up.

My name is Connie. I am seventy-one, and I ran a bowling alley in Wilmington, Delaware for twenty-six years.

When I got my upper plate, nobody warned me about the fire.

Every morning I squeezed paste into the groove.

By noon it turned into a slimy jelly that oozed around the edges.

Every evening I soaked the plate in blue Efferdent tablets at nine dollars a box.

Then I bought four-dollar stiff brushes and scrubbed until my wrists ached.

I even paid thirty-four dollars for a buzzing cleaner from Amazon that died in three weeks.

None of it stopped the fire.

The roof of my mouth was bright crimson and raw.

I sat at Sunday dinner watching my grandkids eat spaghetti while I spooned broth.

I thought this burning was just what dentures felt like.

Then came my checkup with my denturist in Wilmington.

I popped my plate out and handed it to him.

I said, I am sorry for the mess on that plate. I scrubbed it, but that Fixodent glue never really comes off.

He held the plate up and shook his head.

Connie, he said, this plate is loaded with Candida yeast and bacteria.

He told me I had denture stomatitis, just like two-thirds of denture wearers.

Think of an old rubber bath mat on a wet floor, he said.

You paste the plate against your palate. Moisture and body heat get trapped.

Yeast and bacteria burrow into the microscopic pores of the acrylic.

Brushing only scratches the surface, giving yeast deeper grooves to hide in.

And tablets only bleach the outside film.

Every morning you glue it back in, you press an active yeast colony directly against raw tissue.

He told me to test it at home.

Take your plate right after an overnight soak.

Press a clean paper towel hard into the groove.

If it comes away with a yellowish film or smells sour, your cleaner failed.

He told me to get the DentalPULSE Pod.

He said I needed the DentalPULSE Pod because it hits four clinical marks.

First, forty-two thousand Hertz ultrasonic waves to shake biofilm out of the pores.

Second, medical-grade UV-C light to destroy yeast DNA.

Third, plain tap water with zero chemical residue.

Fourth, a solid stainless steel basin.

I ordered the DentalPULSE Pod that afternoon.

When it arrived, I filled the stainless tank with tap water, dropped my plate in, and pressed the button.

Five minutes.

When it stopped, I pulled the lid off.

The water was cloudy, murky brown.

Flecks of stubborn adhesive, bacteria, and cloudy yellow stains were floating in the water.

Gunk that months of scrubbing and fizzy tablets had left behind in the pores.

I slipped the plate in.

It felt completely smooth against my gums, like cool porcelain.

Within four days, the fire cooled down.

By the second week, the raw red patches were gone. My palate was pale, healthy pink again.

Last Tuesday I sliced a ripe beefsteak tomato, salted it, and ate it over the sink.

Not a single twinge of burning.

And the thirty-six tubes of paste under my sink?

I tossed every single one in the trash.

Soaking in tablets and scrubbing with brushes will never clear the bacteria trapped in acrylic pores.
